title: The Western water crisis has a really simple solution
gist: Yglesias argues the U.S. is not water-scarce in aggregate — freshwater per capita is above the global average — but a small, arid Western minority has projected its water anxieties onto the whole country; the real fix is to stop giving most water to farmers for almost nothing, and the Trump administration's cut to Arizona, California, and Nevada is the right call.

insights.claim: The United States is a water-abundant country whose freshwater resources per capita are above the global average, outpacing every other major state except water-rich outliers like Canada and Brazil.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Reframes 'the water crisis' as a regional-allocation problem, not a national scarcity story — relevant to how water-related infrastructure and agriculture risk are priced.
insights.quote: Our freshwater resources per capita are above average globally, and while we’re no Canada or Brazil, we easily outpace the world’s other major states in terms of water availability.
insights.locator: For starters, the United States is a land of relatively abundant water

insights.claim: The U.S. water problem is regional aridity: a sizable majority of the population lives in the well-watered Eastern United States, with far more people living east of the I-35 line running Fort Worth–Oklahoma City–Wichita–Kansas City–Des Moines–Minneapolis than west of it.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Locates the actual scarcity in a minority of the country, implying national water-panic narratives overstate systemic risk.
insights.quote: Way more people live east of that line than west of it, and this historical settlement pattern basically comes down to water availability.
insights.locator: if you look at a map of the United States at night

insights.claim: Air conditioning made arid cities like Las Vegas and Phoenix livable, driving population growth that has intensified water-scarcity issues in the dry part of the country.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Ties Sun Belt migration to a technology-enabled build-out in water-short regions, framing the conflict as self-inflicted growth in the wrong places.
insights.quote: the advent of air conditioning means that places like Las Vegas and Phoenix are now livable, which has created more and more issues around water scarcity
insights.locator: But the Western United States is quite beautiful

insights.claim: There is not enough water in the Colorado River to meet demand, which drives most of the conflicts around Western water use.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Identifies structurally over-allocated supply as the root of Western water disputes, a durable source of legal and political risk for the region.
insights.quote: there just isn’t enough water in the Colorado River to meet demand, and this drives most of the conflicts around water use
insights.locator: A lot of the water used in this dry region

insights.claim: The Trump administration's recent sharp cut to the water available to Arizona, California, and Nevada is the right thing to do, but will intensify Western water conflicts.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Endorses federal supply cuts as correct even as they raise conflict, a signal that allocation fights among the three states will escalate.
insights.quote: Last week the Trump administration sharply cut the water available to Arizona, California, and Nevada. This is, as far as I can tell, the right thing to do.

insights.claim: The simple solution to the Western water crisis is to stop giving the majority of the water away to farmers for almost nothing.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Points the policy lever at agricultural water pricing/allocation rather than conservation by cities — the largest and cheapest source of reallocatable supply.
insights.quote: Stop giving the majority of the water away to farmers for almost nothing!

insights.claim: A small minority living in the arid West has inflicted its water-related neuroses on America as a whole, creating a false impression that the country broadly suffers critical water shortages.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Warns that national water-scarcity discourse is distorted by a regional minority, mispricing the true (localized) nature of the problem.
insights.quote: the relatively small minority of the population that lives in the relevant part of the country has managed to inflict its various water-related neuroses on America as a whole
insights.locator: Part of my annoyance with this discourse
